thresholds.label: Judicial Conference standard for considering an additional district judgeship
thresholds.description: The Judicial Conference's starting point for the district courts is 430 weighted filings per authorized judgeship after accounting for the judgeships it recommends; it generally requires a court to be above 430 to recommend an additional judgeship. It also weighs other factors (senior and magistrate judge assistance, geography, case mix), so crossing 430 is not by itself a recommendation.
thresholds.source: CRS Insight IN12541, "Recommendation for New U.S. Circuit and District Court Judgeships by the Judicial Conference of the United States (119th Congress)"; AO, "Judiciary Makes the Case for New Judgeships" (2020)

thresholds.label: Judicial emergency threshold (with a vacancy)
thresholds.description: A district court vacancy is a judicial emergency when weighted filings exceed 600 per judgeship; a vacancy open more than 18 months is an emergency when weighted filings are 430 to 600 per judgeship; so is a court with more than one authorized judgeship and only one active judge. The definition needs vacancy data, which this server doesn't have, so it can report the filings side only.
thresholds.source: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, "Judicial Emergency Definition"

recommendation.source: Table 1. Additional Judgeships Recommended by the Judicial Conference, 2025

data.statement: N.D. Fla. had 757 weighted filings per authorized judgeship in FY2025 (JB-2025, Table X-1A), above the 430 and 600 thresholds. In 2025 the Judicial Conference recommended 1 additional judgeship for it. This server makes no recommendation of its own.

body.markdown:
# Weighted filings per judgeship

Weighted filings multiply each case by a Federal Judicial Center case weight
(the relative judge time its type needs) and divide the total by authorized
judgeships. The Judicial Conference uses them when it assesses the need for
judgeships: it generally looks for more than 430 per judgeship before
recommending one, and 600 marks a judicial emergency where there is a vacancy.

- Judicial Business Table X-1A publishes them by district, first, for each
  fiscal year. Judicial Facts and Figures Table 6.2 publishes the national
  series over many years.
- Starting with the 2023 edition, Table 6.2 revised the weighted civil series
  down for recent years (FY2020: 554 → 322). The tables' notes don't explain
  why. This server reports both figures with their editions and labels any
  explanation of the revision as inference.
- Territorial courts are outside the case-weight studies, so no weighted
  figures are published for them.
- The current case weights (FJC 2016 study) are not fully published, so
  weighted figures come only from the official tables, never from the IDB.

terms.definition: Filings multiplied by case weights the Federal Judicial Center derives from time studies, so each case counts by the relative judge time its type needs (a death-penalty habeas case weighs far more than a student-loan collection). Weighted filings per judgeship divide the weighted total by authorized judgeships. The Judicial Conference uses them to assess judgeship needs. Current weights come from the FJC's 2016 study; the weights themselves are not fully published.
terms.source: Judicial Business Table X-1A and JFF Table 6.2 notes; FJC

terms.definition: Cases (civil) or defendants (criminal) filed, divided by authorized judgeships, with every case counting once. Table X-1A excludes civil cases reopened, remanded or transferred in by the JPML.

Article III district judgeships authorized by statute, used as the denominator of per-judgeship figures. Table X-1A excludes the territorial courts; JFF Table 6.1 counts them. Districts that share a judgeship show halves (E.D. Ky. 5.5). Vacancies don't reduce the count.

The District Courts of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the Virgin Islands (Article IV courts). They are excluded from the FJC case-weight studies, so Table X-1A publishes no weighted filings for them.

Civil cases with common questions of fact, consolidated before one district (the transferee court) for pretrial proceedings by the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation under 28 U.S.C. § 1407. The IDB marks cases transferred in by the Panel (origin 6) and, from July 1, 2016, cases filed directly in the MDL court (origin 13).

A case filed directly in the MDL (transferee) court instead of being filed elsewhere and transferred by the Panel. The IDB codes it origin 13 from July 1, 2016; before that such cases were origin 1 (original proceeding) and can't be told apart. Direct filing can concentrate tens of thousands of cases in one district in one year, as in N.D. Fla. in FY2020 (MDL 2885, 3M Combat Arms earplugs). Table X-1A counts them as filings in that district.
terms.source: FJC IDB Civil Codebook (origin 13); IDB counts (Phase 2)

terms.definition: A case transferred to the MDL court by the Judicial Panel (origin 6). Table X-1A excludes these from civil filings per judgeship; Table C-1's pending counts include them.
terms.source: FJC IDB Civil Codebook; Tables X-1A and C-1 notes

terms.definition: October 1 to September 30, named for the year it ends: FY2020 ran from October 1, 2019 to September 30, 2020. Every recent table in the catalog reports fiscal years; older rows may be statistical years.

Before the judiciary switched to fiscal-year reporting in the early 1990s, it reported 12-month periods ending June 30 (July 1 to June 30). JFF's 1990 rows are statistical year 1990 (July 1989 to June 1990), so they aren't directly comparable with the fiscal-year rows after them.
terms.source: JFF Tables 6.1–6.3 notes ("Twelve-month period ending June 30")

terms.definition: One publication of a table, such as Judicial Business 2020 (JB-2020) or Judicial Facts and Figures 2023 (JFF-2023). The same statistic for the same year can appear in several editions, sometimes with different values; this server labels every figure with its edition and never mixes them.

A later edition printing a different value for the same measure, court and year than an earlier edition did. Example: FY2020 weighted civil filings per judgeship were 554 in JB-2020 (and JFF 2020–2022) and 322 in JFF-2023 onward. The server returns the latest edition by default and attaches the first-published value.

aliases: judicial business of the united states courts
terms.definition: The Director of the AO's annual report on the courts' work for the fiscal year, with detailed statistical tables (C-1, C-5, X-1A…). It is where a year's figures are first published.
The AO's multi-year summary tables (6.1, 6.2, 6.3 for the district courts), updated each year. They repeat, and sometimes revise, figures first published in Judicial Business.
Judicial Business Table X-1A: weighted and unweighted filings per authorized judgeship for each district court, the source for district-level per-judgeship figures.
Judicial Business Table C-1: civil cases filed, terminated and pending by district and by U.S./private jurisdiction for the fiscal year.
Judicial Business Table C-5: median time from filing to disposition of civil cases by district and stage of disposition.

Judicial Facts and Figures Table 6.2: national weighted and unweighted filings per authorized judgeship over many years. Its 2023 edition revised the weighted civil series for recent years down; the table's notes don't explain why.

Cases open at the end of the period (September 30 for a fiscal year). Table C-1 includes cases transferred in under an MDL order. A later edition can restate the prior year's closing count (FY2017: 339,131 in JB-2017, 366,195 in JB-2018).
Cases closed in the period, by any disposition (dismissal, judgment, transfer, remand, statistical closing). A case reopened and closed again counts as a termination each time.

The median months from filing to disposition for the cases terminated in the period (Table C-5, JFF 6.3). Land condemnations, prisoner petitions, deportation reviews, recovery of overpayments and enforcement of judgments are excluded; not computed for fewer than 10 cases.

The three-digit code for the subject of a civil case (for example 442 employment civil rights, 830 patent). Table C-2 groups the codes into categories (contract, real property, torts, statutes) and groups. Ask about a code ("nature of suit 442") for its label and group.
terms.source: FJC IDB Civil Codebook; Table C-2

terms.definition: The Federal Judicial Center's case-level data on federal cases. This server uses the civil file: every case active in FY2015–FY2025, one row per record, all codes decoded. Judge identifiers are removed by Judicial Conference policy, and party names are never loaded into the server.

Rebuilding a published count (filings, terminations, pending) from the IDB and comparing it with the official table. The result is matched (within tolerance), explained variance (a known, quantified cause such as a restated figure or reopened cases) or unexplained.
A party representing itself without a lawyer. The IDB records whether the plaintiff, the defendant, both or neither were pro se at filing.
A party allowed to proceed without paying the filing fee because of inability to pay. Recorded in the IDB's IFP field.

A disposition code (18) for cases pending over three years with no activity for 12 months and all contemplated proceedings completed; it removes the case from pending counts though it may be reopened.

A vacancy the AO designates an emergency: in a district court, a vacancy where weighted filings exceed 600 per judgeship, a vacancy open more than 18 months where weighted filings are 430–600, or a multi-judgeship court with only one active judge. It depends on vacancies, which this server doesn't track.

The Judicial Conference generally requires more than 430 weighted filings per authorized judgeship before recommending an additional district judgeship (with other factors); 600 marks a judicial emergency where there is a vacancy. The server reports these as context and makes no recommendation.
terms.source: CRS Insight IN12541; AO judicial emergency definition

terms.definition: The basis of federal jurisdiction: U.S. government plaintiff or defendant ("U.S. civil" in Table C-1), or, between private parties, federal question, diversity of citizenship or local question ("private civil").
terms.source: FJC IDB Civil Codebook (JURIS); Table C-1
